topic: Sound for Picture — Post Workflow & Deliverables

fields.definition: A designed sound element—commonly a whoosh, riser, swell, or impact—placed at a picture cut or scene change to smooth or emphasize the visual transition and carry the audience from one shot, scene, or segment to the next.
fields.plain_english: A sound, like a whoosh, played right when the picture cuts to a new scene. It helps the change feel smooth. Think of a page-turn sound telling you the story has moved on.
fields.purpose_function: It bridges edits so scene or segment changes feel intentional and fluid, and it can build energy or signal a shift in time, place, or mood.
fields.practical_application: An editor drops a whoosh or riser on the cut between segments in a trailer, promo, or documentary, timing its peak to the exact frame of the visual change.
common_mistakes: Placing the effect's peak off the actual picture cut so it feels disconnected from the edit
Overusing transitional whooshes until they lose impact and clutter the mix
Failing to match the effect's tone and length to the pace and genre of the piece
scenario_contexts: Adding whooshes between shots in a fast-cut promo or trailer
Bridging chapter or segment changes in a documentary or corporate video
Marking a flashback or time jump in a scripted scene

sources: Ric Viers, The Sound Effects Bible
David Yewdall, Practical Art of Motion Picture Sound

fields.definition: A version of a program's dialogue and narration rendered into a target language, used as the source text for dubbing, voice-over, or subtitle creation during localization.
fields.plain_english: The show's spoken words written out in another language. Voice actors and subtitle makers work from it, like a recipe translated so cooks in another country can make the same dish.
fields.purpose_function: It gives the dubbing director, voice talent, and subtitlers an accurate, timing-aware text so the localized version matches the original meaning and screen action.
fields.practical_application: A localization team receives the translated script and records replacement dialogue or builds subtitle files from it, checking that lines fit the on-screen timing and lip movement.
common_mistakes: Translating word-for-word instead of adapting lines to fit timing and lip sync
Ignoring on-screen text and context that the translation must account for
Assuming one translated script serves both dubbing and subtitles without adaptation
scenario_contexts: Preparing a foreign-language dub of a film for international release
Creating subtitles for a streaming series in several languages
Recording a UN-style voice-over for a documentary interview

fields.definition: A quality-control step in localization where a qualified reviewer checks that a translated script, dub, or subtitle correctly conveys the meaning, tone, and context of the original before the deliverable is approved.
fields.plain_english: A check to make sure the translation really says the same thing as the original. It is like having a second person proofread your work in another language before you hand it in.
fields.purpose_function: It catches mistranslations, missing context, and tone errors so the localized version stays faithful to the original and meets client or broadcaster standards.
fields.practical_application: Before final delivery, a reviewer compares the translated subtitles or dub against the source, flags errors, and sends corrections back to the translator or dubbing team.
common_mistakes: Reviewing only the words without watching the picture for context and on-screen action
Skipping the review to save time, letting errors reach final delivery
Treating personal style preferences as genuine accuracy errors
scenario_contexts: Signing off subtitles before a streaming platform delivery
Checking a dubbed episode's script against the original for a broadcaster
Verifying a translated voice-over for a corporate or training video

fields.definition: In immersive sound for picture, a two-dimensional-to-three-dimensional blend is the balance or control that mixes flat, planar (stereo or surround, 2D) content with height-bearing, object-based (3D/immersive) content, letting a source or bed sit anywhere between a horizontal plane and the full three-dimensional sound field.
fields.plain_english: It sets how much a sound stays flat around you versus wrapping fully above and around you. You dial between plain stereo-style sound and full 3D sound.
fields.purpose_function: It lets mixers move material between legacy 2D formats and immersive 3D formats and control how much height and envelopment a sound has, so one mix can serve both flat and immersive deliverables.
fields.practical_application: Preparing a Dolby Atmos deliverable, a mixer blends a 2D music stem with 3D object placement, adjusting how far elements lift off the horizontal plane into the height speakers.
common_mistakes: Assuming a 2D-to-3D blend is a true upmix - it controls placement and height balance, not added source separation
Pushing everything into 3D height so the mix loses a solid front image and dialogue anchor
Forgetting to check the 2D fold-down, so the stereo or surround deliverable sounds wrong
scenario_contexts: Balancing a stereo music bed against object-based effects in a Dolby Atmos film mix
Deciding how much ambience lifts into height channels for an immersive trailer
Creating both a 5.1 and an immersive deliverable from one session

sources: Dolby Atmos Renderer / Dolby Atmos technical documentation (Dolby Laboratories)
AES - Audio for Virtual and Augmented Reality (aes.org)

fields.definition: A localization technique in which the original speech is kept audible at a low level while a translated voice-over is laid over it, so the audience hears both the source voice and the translation; it is widely used for documentary and news interviews.
fields.plain_english: You still hear the first speaker quietly underneath. A new voice reads the translation over the top. It is the style you often hear in TV news interviews with guests from other countries.
fields.purpose_function: It preserves the authenticity and identity of the original speaker while making the content understandable to a new-language audience, unlike full dubbing which replaces the voice entirely.
fields.practical_application: A post mixer lowers the original interview audio by several dB and rides the translated voice-over on top, usually starting the translation a beat after the original begins.
common_mistakes: Muting the original voice completely, which defeats the purpose of the style
Starting the translation at the exact same instant so the speaker's identity is lost
Setting the original too loud so the translation is hard to follow
scenario_contexts: Translating an on-camera interview in a documentary
Localizing eyewitness testimony in a news package
Voicing a foreign-language speaker in a corporate or factual program

fields.definition: A short designed sound that gives audible feedback for an interaction with a device, app, or on-screen interface—such as a button press, notification, error, or menu move—confirming that an action registered.
fields.plain_english: The little beep or click a phone or app makes when you tap a button or get a message. It tells your ears the device noticed what you did, like a doorbell confirming someone pressed it.
fields.purpose_function: It confirms user actions and signals system state without the user needing to look, which improves usability and accessibility.
fields.practical_application: A sound designer creates and edits sets of clicks, chimes, and alerts for an app, game menu, or product, matching each to its interface event and level-matching them to be noticeable but not annoying.
common_mistakes: Making UI sounds too loud or harsh so they annoy the user
Reusing one generic sound for actions that should feel different
Relying on the sound as the only feedback, ignoring accessibility
scenario_contexts: Designing button and menu sounds for a mobile app
Creating alert and notification tones for a product or device
Adding on-screen interface sounds to a game's menus

sources: Ric Viers, The Sound Effects Bible

fields.definition: A metronome guide for scoring to picture whose tempo changes over time according to a tempo map, letting musical beats and downbeats line up with specific picture hit points instead of staying at one fixed tempo.
fields.plain_english: A count-in click for musicians that speeds up or slows down on purpose. Its tempo shifts so the music lands exactly on key moments in the film, like a drummer changing pace to match the action.
fields.purpose_function: It lets a composer and players hit precise on-screen events—a punch, a door slam, a cut—while staying in time, by mapping tempo changes to those cue points.
fields.practical_application: A composer builds a tempo map in a DAW with tempo changes and streamers or punches, then musicians perform to that variable click so downbeats align with the picture.
common_mistakes: Confusing a variable click with a fixed-tempo click that never changes
Placing tempo changes carelessly so hits land off the picture
Not warning players before a tempo change so they fall out of time
scenario_contexts: Recording an orchestral film cue that must hit several action beats
Scoring a scene where the music must slow for an emotional moment
Syncing a live ensemble to picture on a scoring stage

sources: Fred Karlin & Rayburn Wright, On the Track: A Guide to Contemporary Film Scoring
Frans Absil, Film and Video Game Music technical notes

fields.definition: A category of sound effect covering the noises made by cars, trucks, motorcycles, and other vehicles—engine, tires, doors, brakes, pass-bys—recorded or designed and edited to match on-screen vehicles.
fields.plain_english: The sounds a car or other vehicle makes on screen, like the engine, tires, and doors. Editors add or replace them so the vehicle you see matches the vehicle you hear.
fields.purpose_function: It gives on-screen vehicles believable, matched sound, supporting realism and storytelling—a roaring engine for a chase, a quiet idle for tension.
fields.practical_application: A sound editor cuts recorded engine, tire, and door sounds, or library effects, to picture, syncing starts, stops, gear changes, and pass-bys to the vehicle's action.
common_mistakes: Using an engine sound that does not match the type of vehicle on screen
Ignoring perspective, so a distant car sounds as loud as a close one
Forgetting the Doppler pitch shift on fast pass-bys
scenario_contexts: Cutting engine and tire sounds for a car-chase scene
Adding a car door and start for a character driving off
Building traffic backgrounds for a city street scene

sources: Ric Viers, The Sound Effects Bible
David Yewdall, Practical Art of Motion Picture Sound

fields.definition: A virtual-reality audio room is a software-simulated acoustic environment - with modeled room geometry, reflections, and reverberation plus head-tracked 3D source positioning - in which a sound designer auditions, places, and mixes spatial audio for VR or other immersive content.
fields.plain_english: It is a pretend room inside software where you place sounds in 3D and hear them as they would sound in VR. You can move your head and the sound moves with the scene.
fields.purpose_function: It lets creators design and check how audio will behave inside a head-tracked virtual space before release, so sources sit in the right place and the room's echoes match the visual environment.
fields.practical_application: A VR sound designer loads a scene into a virtual-reality audio room, positions ambiences and effects around the listener, and monitors on head-tracked headphones to confirm the mix holds up as the viewer looks around.
common_mistakes: Mixing only on speakers and skipping head-tracked headphone checks, so the VR experience differs from the mix
Ignoring the modeled room's reverb so sound does not match the visual space
Placing sources without checking behind and above the listener
scenario_contexts: Positioning ambisonic ambience for a 360 video in a virtual room
Auditioning a VR game scene's audio with head tracking before build
Matching modeled room reverb to a virtual environment's size and materials

sources: AES - Audio for Virtual and Augmented Reality (aes.org)
Sennheiser AMBEO / dearVR SPATIAL CONNECT technical documentation
